name: Combinations with repetition
seoDesc: Combinations with repetition: answer 5 values and the page computes the result when you press Calculate — formula and worked example included.
summary: The Combinations with repetition calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports combinations with repetitions immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. It is built for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Combinations with repetition calculator work?
sections.html:
The Combinations with repetition calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports combinations with repetitions in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the figures it asks for.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Combinations with repetition calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Combinations with repetitions=(total number of objects n + sample size r) ÷ ((total number of objects n) × (sample size r + 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Total number of objects n = 10 and Sample size r = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Combinations with repetitions = 92378.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Combinations with repetitions = 92378 should be roughly the size you expected from Total number of objects n = 10 and Sample size r = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Combinations with repetition calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Combinations with repetition calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — total number of objects n for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Combinations with repetition calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns combinations with repetitions. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Combinations with repetition calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Combinations with repetitions = 92378. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Combinations with repetition calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
